excerpt: Section 1, The Discrete Kalman Filter Algorithm (paraphrased for practice). The filter estimates the state x of a process governed by x_k = A x_{k-1} + B u_{k-1} + w_{k-1} from measurements z_k = H x_k + v_k, where the process noise w and measurement noise v are independent, white and normal with covariances Q and R. Each step has a time update (predict) and a measurement update (correct). Time update: the a priori estimate is x̂⁻_k = A x̂_{k-1} + B u_{k-1} and its error covariance is P⁻_k = A P_{k-1} Aᵀ + Q (equations 1.9 and 1.10). Measurement update: the Kalman gain K_k = P⁻_k Hᵀ (H P⁻_k Hᵀ + R)⁻¹ (1.11); the a posteriori estimate x̂_k = x̂⁻_k + K_k (z_k − H x̂⁻_k) (1.12); and P_k = (I − K_k H) P⁻_k (1.13). The difference z_k − H x̂⁻_k is called the innovation or residual. As the measurement noise covariance R approaches zero the gain weights the residual more heavily, so the actual measurement is trusted more; as the a priori error covariance P⁻_k approaches zero the gain weights the residual less, so the prediction is trusted more. Section 3 estimates a scalar random constant (A = 1, H = 1, no control input) from noisy measurements.
focus: Explain the scalar Kalman filter (A = 1, H = 1, no control input) estimating a constant from a short, fixed sequence of noisy measurements. Let the learner change the measurement noise R, the process noise Q and the initial error covariance P₀. Show, for each step, the prediction, the gain K, the innovation z − x̂⁻, the corrected estimate and P. Guide them through (a) very small R, where the estimate follows the measurements, and (b) very large R, where the estimate barely moves. Check that 0 ≤ K ≤ 1 at every step and that P never increases during a measurement update.
audience: Third-year engineering undergraduates who know basic probability (mean, variance) but have not seen state estimation.
